title: Lesson 5: Regression, Linearity & Dose-Response
text:
In Lesson 4 you decided how to code your exposure. This lesson puts that exposure into a regression model: choosing a model based on your outcome, interpreting the estimate it produces, and checking whether the assumption that the exposure is related to the outcome “in a straight line” actually holds. It has two parts:
Both parts end with a 🧠 Your Turn for the exposure and outcome in your own project. Together they produce the crude model and the evaluation of functional form that Milestone 2 asks for.

section: Step 1: What kind of outcome do you have — and is it rare or common?
text:
Step 1: What kind of outcome do you have — and is it rare or common?
The type of outcome determines the model. high_blood_pressure is binary (1 = diagnosed, 0 = not), so a linear regression model is not appropriate — we need logistic or log-binomial regression. Which of those two to prefer depends on whether the outcome is rare or common.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Questions to consider:

What proportion of participants have high blood pressure? Would you call that rare or common?
How many participants are missing this outcome?







Note💡 Answers — click to reveal after you’ve thought about it






About 30% of participants with data (606 of 1,988) have high blood pressure. That is a common outcome — a rough rule of thumb is that an outcome is “rare” if it affects fewer than about 10% of people.
12 participants are missing high_blood_pressure. R will drop them automatically from every model below, so all models are fit on the 1,988 participants with data.

title: Lesson 5: Regression, Linearity & Dose-Response
section: Step 2: A two-by-two table you can calculate by hand
text:
Step 2: A two-by-two table you can calculate by hand
Before fitting any model, let’s calculate the association the old-fashioned way, so you can see exactly what the regression model will reproduce. We’ll use tree canopy dichotomized at the median — the same kind of binary exposure you created in Lesson 4.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
What each step of the code does:

Create a binary exposure. median(hrlctree, na.rm = TRUE) finds the median tree canopy value (about 0.12, or 12%); na.rm = TRUE tells R to ignore any missing values when doing so. ifelse() then checks each participant: if their tract’s canopy is above the median, the new variable tree_high is set to 1 (“high canopy”); otherwise it is set to 0 (“low canopy”). mutate() adds tree_high to the data as a new column, leaving hrlctree unchanged.
Build the two-by-two table. table() counts how many participants fall into each combination of tree_high (the rows) and high_blood_pressure (the columns). The names before the = signs (Tree_high, HBP) are just labels for the printed table. Typing two_by_two on its own line prints it. Participants missing high_blood_pressure are left out of the table.
Save the four counts. Each line stores one cell of the table under a letter — A, B, C, or D — so that we can use it in the formulas that follow. The numbers in square brackets tell R which cell to take: the first is the row and the second is the column. The table below the code shows which group of people each letter represents.
Calculate the prevalence in each group. Prevalence is the number of people with the outcome divided by everyone in that group. Among high-canopy participants that is A / (A + B); among low-canopy participants it is C / (C + D).
Calculate the measures of association. The prevalence ratio divides the prevalence in the high-canopy group by the prevalence in the low-canopy group. The odds ratio is the cross-product (A × D) / (B × C). c() combines the four results into one labeled list, so they print together.

Each of the four cells in the table counts a different group of people:









High blood pressure (HBP = 1)
No high blood pressure (HBP = 0)




High canopy (tree_high = 1)
A = people in high-canopy tracts with high blood pressure
B = people in high-canopy tracts without high blood pressure


Low canopy (tree_high = 0)
C = people in low-canopy tracts with high blood pressure
D = people in low-canopy tracts without high blood pressure



Note that R prints the table with the 0 (low canopy, no high blood pressure) row and column first, so the printed table is arranged D, C / B, A — which is why the code picks each count out by position.






NotePrevalence, not risk



Because the class dataset is a cross-sectional survey — everyone was surveyed at one point in time — we are comparing the prevalence of high blood pressure (who has it now), not the risk of developing it over follow-up. That is why we call this a prevalence ratio rather than a risk ratio.


Questions to consider:

What is the prevalence of high blood pressure in each canopy group?
Is the prevalence ratio (PR) or the odds ratio (OR) further from the null value of 1? Why does that happen with an outcome this common?







Note💡 Answers — click to reveal after you’ve thought about it






The prevalence is 25.5% in high-canopy tracts (252 of 987) and 35.4% in low-canopy tracts (354 of 1,001).
PR = 0.255 / 0.354 = 0.72; OR = 0.63. The OR is further from the null. Odds are prevalence divided by one minus prevalence, p / (1 − p). When p is small, 1 − p is close to 1, so odds and prevalence are nearly the same. When p is large (here, around 0.3), dividing by 1 − p stretches the odds away from the prevalence, and the OR ends up further from 1 than the PR. Describing the OR of 0.63 as if it were a PR would overstate how much lower high blood pressure is in greener tracts.

title: Lesson 5: Regression, Linearity & Dose-Response
section: Step 3: The same comparison as a regression model
text:
Step 3: The same comparison as a regression model
Now, we will make the same comparison, running both a logistic and a log-binomial regression model. We will use the results from these models to calculate the odds ratio and its 95% confidence interval (CI), and the prevalence ratio and its 95% CI.
The two models differ only in their link function — what the model treats as a straight-line function of the exposure:

Logistic regression, binomial(link = "logit"), models the log odds of the outcome.
Log-binomial regression, binomial(link = "log"), models the log prevalence.







NoteWhy do we exponentiate the coefficient and the CI?



Because both models work on the log scale, the coefficient R reports for tree_high is not a ratio — it is a difference in logs. For the log-binomial model:

log(prevalence in high-canopy tracts) = β₀ + β₁
log(prevalence in low-canopy tracts) = β₀
the difference, β₁, is log(prevalence high) − log(prevalence low) = log(PR)

To get back from log(PR) to the PR itself, we undo the log by exponentiating: PR = exp(β₁). (The same logic applied to log odds gives OR = exp(β₁) for the logistic model.)
The 95% CI is built on the same log scale, as β₁ ± 1.96 × SE, so we exponentiate its two endpoints the same way: exp(β₁ − 1.96 × SE) and exp(β₁ + 1.96 × SE). That is also why ratio CIs are not symmetric around the estimate — they are symmetric on the log scale, not on the ratio scale.


The extract_ratio() helper below does these steps for us: it pulls out each coefficient and its standard error, then exponentiates the coefficient and both CI endpoints. It is the same idea as the extract_or() function from Lesson 4, just renamed because it now produces prevalence ratios as well as odds ratios.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Questions to consider:

Compare each estimate to the one you calculated by hand in Step 2. Do they match?
Write a one-sentence interpretation of the PR and its 95% CI.







Note💡 Answers — click to reveal after you’ve written your own






Yes — the logistic model’s OR (0.63) and the log-binomial model’s PR (0.72) match the two-by-two table exactly. A crude model with a single binary exposure is doing the same calculation as the table; what the model adds is a confidence interval, and (from next week) the ability to adjust for other variables.
Example interpretation: The prevalence of high blood pressure among participants living in census tracts with tree canopy above the median was 0.72 times the prevalence among those living in tracts at or below the median (95% CI: 0.63, 0.83) — about 28% lower. Because the whole CI is below 1, the data are not consistent with no association (a PR of 1).

title: Lesson 5: Regression, Linearity & Dose-Response
section: Step 4: Entering the exposure as a continuous term
text:
Step 4: Entering the exposure as a continuous term
Dichotomizing at the median throws away information. By creating a binary variable in this way, we are in essence treating someone who lives in a census tract with 13% tree canopy coverage (just greater than the median) the same as someone living in a tract with ~63% coverage (the maximum of the distribution). Entering hrlctree as a continuous term uses all the information available. But recall that hrlctree is a proportion (0 to 1), so a “one-unit increase” would mean going from 0% to 100% canopy — a meaningless comparison. We rescale by multiplying by 100, so that the exposure is a percentage (0 to 100) and a one-unit increase means a one-percentage-point increase in tree canopy cover (for example, from 12% to 13%).

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Questions to consider:

Interpret the PR per one-percentage-point increase in tree canopy.
This model assumes that every one-point increase — from 5% to 6%, or from 40% to 41% — multiplies prevalence by the same amount. Is that a reasonable assumption?







Note💡 Answers — click to reveal after you’ve thought about it






Each one-percentage-point increase in census-tract tree canopy cover was associated with a 2.7% lower prevalence of high blood pressure (PR = 0.973; 95% CI: 0.964, 0.983). Because the PR for a single percentage point is close to 1, report it to three decimal places so the estimate and CI are distinguishable.
A one-point change is small relative to the range of canopy (about 2% to 63%). Because the model multiplies the PR for each additional point, you can also describe a larger contrast by raising the PR to that power: for a 10-point increase, 0.973¹⁰ ≈ 0.76, or about 24% lower prevalence. (In R: exp(10 * coef(model_cont)[2]).) The model and its assumptions are the same; only the size of the comparison you report changes.
We can’t tell from this model — a single continuous term will return one PR no matter what the true shape of the relationship is. That is exactly what Part 2 checks.










Note💡 What if my log-binomial model won’t converge?





Log-binomial models sometimes fail with an error like “no valid set of coefficients has been found: please supply starting values”. This happens because predicted prevalences must stay below 1, which the fitting algorithm can struggle with — especially when an exposure has a few extremely high values. Two common fixes:

Supply starting values. Set the intercept to the log of the overall prevalence and the other coefficients to 0, e.g. start = c(log(0.3), 0) for a model with one exposure term.
Use a modified Poisson model — a Poisson model with robust (“sandwich”) standard errors, which also estimates a prevalence ratio.

Code: running a modified Poisson model (in RStudio)
# Packages for robust ("sandwich") standard errors -- install once with install.packages()
library(sandwich)
library(lmtest)

# Fit a Poisson model with a log link (same outcome and exposure as the log-binomial model)
model_pois <- glm(high_blood_pressure ~ hrlctree_pct, data = data,
                  family = poisson(link = "log"))

# Replace the usual standard errors with robust ones
robust_se <- vcovHC(model_pois, type = "HC0")

coeftest(model_pois, vcov = robust_se)      # coefficients with robust SEs
exp(coef(model_pois))                       # PR point estimate
exp(coefci(model_pois, vcov = robust_se))   # PR 95% CI










Tip🧠 Your Turn: Fit a crude model for your own project



Using the exposure and outcome from your project (and the exposure coding you decided on in Lesson 4):

Check whether your outcome is binary or continuous and, if binary, how common it is.
Fit the appropriate crude model: log-binomial (or logistic, if you can justify it) for a binary outcome, or lm() for a continuous one. If your exposure is continuous and a one-unit change isn’t meaningful (e.g., it’s a proportion), rescale it first.
Use extract_ratio() to get your estimate and 95% CI (skip the exponentiating for a linear model — use coef() and confint() instead), and write a one-sentence interpretation.

Note💡 Example: traffic density (ctb1traff) and asthma — click to reveal






Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Interpretation: the prevalence of asthma among participants living in census tracts with traffic density above the median was 1.81 times the prevalence among those in tracts at or below the median (95% CI: 1.37, 2.38).
Asthma affects only about 10% of participants, so the OR (1.93) and PR are closer to each other here than they were for high blood pressure — the rarer the outcome, the better the OR approximates the PR.
Why dichotomize rather than enter traffic as a continuous term? Traffic density is very right-skewed — a handful of tracts have traffic many times higher than everyone else — and a log-binomial model with continuous traffic fails to converge for exactly the reason described in the “won’t converge” box above. The quartile approach in Part 2 is another way to handle it.

section: Steps 1 and 2: Quartiles as indicator terms
text:
Steps 1 and 2: Quartiles as indicator terms

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Wrapping the quartile variable in factor() is what tells R to create a separate indicator term for each category. Without it, R treats 1, 2, 3, 4 as a continuous number and returns a single coefficient — which would assume linearity instead of testing it. The first level (Q1, lowest canopy) is the reference category and drops out of the model; every PR is a comparison with Q1.

title: Lesson 5: Regression, Linearity & Dose-Response
text:
Step 3: Plot the estimates
We plot each quartile’s PR, with Q1 fixed at 1, against the quartile itself. Each quartile gets the same amount of space on the x-axis, so you can see directly how much the PR changes from one quartile to the next. The canopy range of each quartile is shown under its label.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
The y-axis is on a log scale because the log-binomial model is linear on the log scale: if the linearity assumption holds, the PRs should step down (or up) by about the same amount from each quartile to the next.
Questions to consider:

Do Q1, Q2, and Q3 look different from each other? Where does most of the change happen?
Does the line fall at a steady rate across the quartiles, or does it stay flat and then drop?
Now look at the canopy ranges under each label. How does the width of Q4 change your reading of the “drop”?
Given this plot, would you keep tree canopy as a single continuous term, use the quartile categories, or collapse some categories together?







Note💡 Discussion — click to reveal after you’ve looked at the plot yourself





Q2 is essentially the same as Q1, Q3 is slightly lower, and Q4 is much lower (PR ≈ 0.58). On this plot the line is roughly flat from Q1 to Q3 and then drops sharply to Q4 — not the steady, equal-sized steps we would expect if the linearity assumption held. That is a sign the assumption may not hold.
The canopy ranges add an important caveat. The quartiles are equal-sized groups of people, not equal-width ranges of canopy: Q1–Q3 together cover only about 2% to 18% canopy, while Q4 alone covers about 18% to 63%. Part of the “sudden drop” is simply that Q4 contains a much wider — and much greener — range of tracts. Measured in canopy percentage points, the decline above roughly 10% canopy is more gradual than this plot makes it look. This is why it is always worth checking what range of the exposure each category covers before interpreting the shape.
There is no single right answer about what to do next — reasonable options include:

Keep the continuous term, if you judge the departure from linearity to be small. It is the most efficient and easiest to communicate (one PR per percentage point of canopy).
Collapse categories that look alike. Here, Q1–Q3 could be combined into one reference group and compared with Q4 (the top quartile): fewer coefficients, and the estimate reflects where the change actually appears.
Use a flexible term such as a spline (optional section below).

Whatever you choose, justify it using the plot, your sample size in each category, and what will be most meaningful for your research question.

title: Lesson 5: Regression, Linearity & Dose-Response
section: Optional: relaxing linearity with a spline
text:
Optional: relaxing linearity with a spline
You will not be required to use splines in this course, but they are common in environmental epidemiology (for example, temperature–mortality curves). A natural cubic spline lets the relationship bend smoothly instead of forcing a straight line. df sets how flexible the curve is.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.






NoteWhy doesn’t the “linear” model look like a straight line?



In the first plot, the curve labeled “Linear” bends. That’s because the log-binomial model is linear in the log of prevalence, not in prevalence itself: log(P) = β₀ + β₁ × canopy. Undoing the log gives P = exp(β₀ + β₁ × canopy), which is a curve — each additional percentage point of canopy multiplies prevalence by the same amount (the PR), rather than subtracting the same amount. In the second plot, with the y-axis on a log scale, the “Linear” model is a straight line. The linearity assumption we are checking is always about the scale the model works on — here, the log scale.


Question to consider: the spline and the linear model have almost identical AIC values. What does that suggest about how much the linearity assumption actually matters for this particular exposure and outcome?






Note💡 Answer — click to reveal after you’ve thought about it





The spline allows the curve to bend wherever the data suggest, yet it fits the data no better than a single straight line on the log scale (the AICs differ by less than 1). The two curves differ mainly at the lowest canopy values, where the spline levels off, and slightly at the highest values, where few participants live. So, for tree canopy and high blood pressure, the linearity assumption appears to be a reasonable approximation, and a continuous term (per percentage point of canopy) is a defensible choice. The quartile plot is still valuable: it shows where along the canopy range the association is concentrated.










Tip🧠 Your Turn: Check linearity for your own exposure

Create quartiles (or quintiles, if your sample size allows) of your exposure with ntile(), wrapped in factor(), and look at the range of your exposure within each category.
Fit your crude model with the categorical exposure and extract the estimates.
Plot the estimates by category, with the reference category fixed at 1 (or at 0 for a linear model — and use a regular, not log, y-axis).
In two or three sentences, state whether the linearity assumption looks reasonable and what coding you will use in your models going forward.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Compared with Q1 (the lowest-traffic quarter of participants), asthma prevalence is similar in Q2 (PR 1.09), somewhat higher in Q3 (PR 1.35; CI includes 1), and more than twice as high in Q4 (PR 2.41; 95% CI: 1.65, 3.53). The rise is steepest at the top, so a continuous term may not capture the shape well; the quartile categories, or the top quartile vs. the rest, are reasonable choices.

title: Lesson 3: Exploratory Data Analysis & Data Cleaning
text:
In our last session (Lesson 1), we read in and manipulated our data set, and merged in NDVI (greenness) data by census tract. This week’s module is about research questions, conceptual frameworks, and descriptive analysis — you’ve already worked through hypothesis components (exposure, outcome, population, expected relationship) and the mediator-vs-modifier distinction in this week’s “Learn” material. This tutorial is the Practice half: hands-on descriptive statistics, data cleaning, and visualization in R.
That’s not busywork. Every study population, exposure, and outcome needs to be characterized before it can be modeled — and this week’s skills are exactly what you’ll need for Project Milestone 1 (research question, hypothesis, and conceptual framework), due this week. Milestone 1 asks you to start characterizing the exposure and outcome you’re considering for your own project, using this same class dataset. Everything below — checking distributions, spotting errors, visualizing a relationship — is directly reusable for that.
Just as in Lesson 1, we first load any packages we need, then read in our data — using file.path() and the same data_raw / data_processed structure from your EOH635_project, not setwd(). (Recall from Lesson 1: on your own computer you’re responsible for install.packages() and library() for every package you use — this tutorial page loads tidyverse for you automatically, which your own script won’t do.)

What variables have missing values?

Note💡 Compare against the codebook — click to reveal





The Data Codebook lists the missingness that was deliberately built into this simulated dataset: mental_health (42), current_smoker (20), high_blood_pressure (12), stress (7), has_park (5), age (3), gender (2). If your colSums(is.na(data)) output matches that, your merge from Lesson 1 didn’t introduce (or lose) any missingness — which is exactly the kind of check worth doing after any merge.
A caveat specific to this class exercise: we can check against the codebook here only because this is a teaching dataset, built with a known amount of missingness baked in on purpose. With real-world data, you typically don’t know in advance how much missingness you have, or where — you find out by running exactly the code above and looking at the result. A codebook for a real dataset will usually tell you what a variable means and how it’s coded, but not necessarily how much of it is missing in the specific file you were handed.



For now we will not recode any of our missing variables. In some cases it makes sense to recode missing variables — particularly if we can infer their values from other variables in the data frame — but for now we’ll proceed without doing that. It’s good to be aware of which variables have missing values, since we’ll need to think about this later when conducting analyses.
Since you’ll be working with these data in your project analysis, be sure to take note of the variables that have missing values.

title: Lesson 3: Exploratory Data Analysis & Data Cleaning
text:
Checking for Logical Inconsistencies
Missing data is easy to spot — R shows you NA directly. Logical inconsistencies are sneakier. When there’s a logical inconsistency, every individual value can look perfectly plausible on its own — it’s only when you look at two variables together that you find a combination that can’t both be true. A classic example from environmental health survey data: someone recorded as biological sex “male” who also reports an age at first menstruation. Neither value looks wrong in isolation — the problem only shows up when you look at both at once.
The tool for catching this is one you already know: table(), applied to two variables instead of one, to see every combination that actually occurs in the data.
As a quick illustration of the technique (not a real inconsistency — just showing the mechanics), let’s break age into two rough groups and cross it with gender. We’ll use the same approach Lesson 1 used to create r_age and num_education — ifelse(), checking a condition and returning one value if it’s TRUE, another if it’s FALSE:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
What’s happening here: ifelse(data$age < 40, "Under 40", "40 or older") checks every value of data$age — wherever it’s less than 40, it returns the text "Under 40"; everywhere else, it returns "40 or older". That gives us a new vector of labels the same length as data$age, which we store as age_group_demo. table() then cross-tabulates that new label against gender, one count per combination.
Reading a two-way table like this: each cell is a count of people with that combination of both variables. If a cell that should be logically impossible has a nonzero count, that’s your signal to investigate.






Tip🧠 Your Turn



Let’s build a real check, not just an illustration. Think about education: is it possible for someone to have a Bachelor’s degree at age 20? Sure — early admission, an accelerated program, it happens, though it’s uncommon. What about age 19? Now it’s genuinely rare — not a strict logical impossibility the way “male” + “reports menses” is, but rare enough that finding several such cases in one dataset should make you suspicious of a coding error, not assume you’ve found a bunch of prodigies.
Using the same ifelse() pattern as above, build a two-way table crossing an “under 19 / 19 and older” age split against education.

The “Under 19” row should show 0 people with “Bachelor’s degree or higher.” Unlike the strict logical-impossibility example earlier (menses age recorded for someone coded male), this isn’t a constraint that’s guaranteed to hold in every real dataset — it’s a “should be at or near zero; investigate anything that isn’t” check. That distinction matters: not every consistency check has a clean yes/no answer, and part of the skill is judging how surprising a violation would actually be.

title: Lesson 3: Exploratory Data Analysis & Data Cleaning
text:
Visual Exploration of Data
Tables and summary statistics are useful, but it can also be very helpful to visually inspect the distribution of a variable — some patterns (an outlier, an unexpected cluster, a skew) are far easier to spot in a plot than in a column of numbers. Let’s plot some key variables to understand their distributions and relationships.

Example 1: Histogram
Histograms are useful for visualizing the distribution of a single numeric variable. Let’s look at age.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
How to read this: the x-axis is age, split into 5-year bins (that’s what binwidth = 5 does); the y-axis is a count — how many participants fall into each bin. Taller bars mean more people at that age range. From this single plot, you can read off roughly where the minimum and maximum ages are (the leftmost and rightmost bars with any height at all), and see at a glance where the bulk of participants’ ages fall — which, here, looks like it’s concentrated in the younger-to-middle adult range, with progressively fewer people as age increases. You should also be able to spot a bar (or bars) sitting well off to the right, separated from the rest of the distribution — that’s a visual signal of an age outlier, the same implausible values we’re about to deal with directly below.

One thing you’ll need to change: binwidth. A binwidth of 5 made sense for age, which spans roughly 18 to 116 years — but hrlctree is a proportion, ranging only from 0 to 1. More generally, whenever you build a histogram of a new variable: first check its rough range (a quick summary() or range() will tell you), then pick a binwidth that divides that range into something like 10–30 bins. Too few bins hides the shape of the distribution; too many makes it look noisy. There’s no single “correct” binwidth — this is a judgment call you refine by trying a value, looking at the plot, and adjusting.

Note💡 Why as.character()? — click to reveal





high_blood_pressure is stored as an integer 0/1 flag, not a category. Without as.character(), ggplot treats it as a continuous numeric axis and tries to draw a single boxplot (or a strange, mostly-empty range of “groups” between 0 and 1) rather than two separate boxes for “0” and “1”. Summary of numerical variables

What summary statistics does this function produce?
What do you observe about key variables?
Are there particular variables for which these summary statistics do not make sense? (Hint: think about what summary() does with a 0/1 variable versus a truly continuous one like age.)

Think through these for a couple of variables yourself before checking below.






Note💡 Two worked examples — click to reveal





age (a genuinely continuous variable): summary() gives six numbers — Min. 18.02, 1st Qu. 29.99, Median 40.36, Mean 44.99, 3rd Qu. 56.24, Max. 116.00 — plus a count of missing values (NA's 3). These are all meaningful here: the middle 50% of participants (between the 1st and 3rd quartiles) are roughly 30 to 56 years old. But that Max. of 116 should catch your eye immediately — a plausible age tops out well below that. That’s exactly the kind of thing summary() is good for catching early, before it quietly distorts an analysis later. (We’ll deal with this specific outlier in Lesson 3.)
high_blood_pressure (a binary 0/1 flag, not a continuous quantity): summary() reports Min. 0, Median 0, Mean 0.3048, Max. 1. The Min./Median/Max. here aren’t wrong, exactly, but they’re not very useful — a variable that can only be 0 or 1 doesn’t have a meaningful “middle” or “spread” the way age does. The one number worth keeping from this output is the Mean, 0.3048 — for a 0/1 variable, the mean is just the proportion coded 1, so about 30.5% of participants have high blood pressure. For everything else about a binary variable’s distribution, a frequency count (table(), coming up in Section 6) is the right tool, not summary().

text:
Creating a numeric version of the education variable
Right now, education is a character variable — useful for reading and for table(), but not for most quantitative work. Regression models, correlations, and most statistical functions in R need numeric input — they can’t compute something like a mean, a correlation coefficient, or a regression slope on the text strings "< Bachelor's" and "Bachelor's degree or higher". To use education status as a predictor or outcome in that kind of analysis later in the course, we first need a consistently coded numeric (here, binary 0/1) version. Let’s do this now, using base R’s ifelse():






Note



A note for later in the course: if you only ever plan to use education as an explanatory variable (a predictor) in a regression model — not as the outcome — converting it to a numeric 0/1 variable isn’t your only option. R’s regression functions (like lm() and glm()) can also take a factor variable directly as a predictor, and will automatically create the 0/1 coding behind the scenes (this is called “dummy coding”). For a variable with just two categories like this one, numeric 0/1 and factor give you the same result either way. The numeric approach shown here is worth learning first because it makes that dummy-coding step explicit rather than hidden — but once you’re comfortable with what’s happening, factor() is often the more natural choice for a categorical predictor, especially one with more than two levels.



Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
What happened here? This line creates a new variable called num_education, a numeric version of education, using ifelse():

The code checks each value of education.
If the value is "< Bachelor's" (less than a bachelor’s degree), num_education is set to 0.
For all other values (presumably at least a bachelor’s degree), num_education is set to 1.

So this line recodes a categorical education variable into a binary (0/1) numeric variable, where:

0 = less than a bachelor’s degree
1 = bachelor’s degree or higher

Note: in R there are lots of ways to do the same thing. Another way to recode this variable is with the dplyr package (loaded as part of tidyverse) instead of base R’s ifelse().
Quick reminder of the syntax before you try it: mutate() adds (or changes) a column in a data frame, and if_else() works like ifelse() — a condition, then the value to use when it’s TRUE, then the value to use when it’s FALSE. Put together, the general pattern looks like:
data <- data %>%
  mutate(new_column_name = if_else(some_condition, value_if_true, value_if_false))






Tip🧠 Your Turn



dplyr’s equivalent of ifelse() is if_else(), typically used inside mutate(). Try rewriting the num_education recode above using data %>% mutate(...) and if_else() instead of base R. Call the new column num_education2 so you can compare it to the original.

Negative values represent water.
Values close to 1 mean dense vegetation.
Values close to 0 mean a lack of vegetation (there might instead be lots of concrete).

Summarize the NDVI values across Philadelphia
Using our Philadelphia tract-level data frame, let’s look at the distribution of NDVI across the city of Philadelphia.

What is the minimum NDVI value? What does this tell you?
What’s the median? What’s the max?


Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.

But we want to know how green the neighborhoods of our study participants are.
To do so, we’re going to link the NDVI data frame to our primary data frame using a common variable found in both.

The common variable is called geoid10. In our class data frame, geoid10 refers to the census tract in which the study participant lives. In the NDVI data frame, GEOID10 refers to each unique Philadelphia census tract.
In order for the merge/linkage to work, both variables have to be in the same format (both character, or both numeric, etc.). Let’s check on this now.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Notice these don’t match: data$geoid10 shows up as chr, because we deliberately converted it back in Section 5 (it’s a label, not a quantity, remember?) — but PHL_NDVI_summer_annual$GEOID10 is freshly read in from its own file and is still num. This is exactly the situation the earlier conversion was setting up: without it, both would have looked numeric and matched by coincidence, hiding the fact that ID columns need this treatment at all. Since they don’t match now, let’s convert GEOID10 to character too:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
(Re-running data$geoid10 <- as.character(data$geoid10) here as well wouldn’t hurt anything — converting an already-character column to character is a harmless no-op — but it’s only necessary for the one that’s still numeric.)
Now let’s merge the datasets, using a left join:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Now the data frame called data2 should have all of our original variables, plus the variables from the NDVI data frame.
As a check, think about how many variables were in each separate data frame.

How many rows are in data2?

We’re specifically checking this because a left join (all.x = TRUE) is supposed to keep every row from data — one row per participant, no more and no fewer — while just adding columns from PHL_NDVI_summer_annual onto each one. If the row count in data2 doesn’t match the row count in data (2,000), that’s a red flag: it would mean the merge either dropped some participants, or duplicated some (which happens if the NDVI file accidentally has more than one row per geoid10 — each extra match creates an extra output row). Checking nrow() before and after any merge is one of the simplest, most important habits for confirming a merge did what you expected.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Or we can use dim(), which shows us rows and columns:

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
We can also look at the names of the variables in the merged data frame — is everything in there?

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
It’s also helpful to look at the top rows of the merged data frame, to be sure we don’t have a bunch of missing values (coded NA) — if we see missings in the NDVI variables, that likely means something went wrong with our merge!

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
We can also do some logic checks to be sure everything checks out.






Tip🧠 Your Turn



Do participants living in the identical census tract get assigned the same NDVI value? Write code to check this — for example, group data2 by geoid10 and count the number of distinct X2015_NDVI values within each tract. If the merge worked correctly, every tract should have exactly 1 distinct NDVI value.
Why should that be true? X2015_NDVI is a tract-level measurement — it describes the neighborhood, not the individual person. A left join doesn’t create new NDVI values; it just looks up the one value that belongs to each participant’s geoid10 and copies it onto every row that matches. So everyone sharing a tract should end up with the identical copied value. If any tract shows more than one distinct value, something’s wrong — most likely a formatting issue (like the one we just fixed) that caused some participants to match the wrong row, or a duplicate tract entry in the NDVI file itself.
(Hint: dplyr’s group_by(), summarize(), and n_distinct() are useful here.)



Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.






Note💡 Solution — click to reveal






Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
What this output is telling you: the summarize() step produces one row per tract, giving the number of distinct NDVI values found within it (n_unique_ndvi) — then count(n_unique_ndvi) collapses that down into a small frequency table, showing how many tracts (n) had each possible value of n_unique_ndvi. What you’re looking for is a single row: n_unique_ndvi = 1, with n equal to the total number of tracts (384) — meaning every tract, without exception, has exactly one NDVI value. If you instead saw a second row (e.g., n_unique_ndvi = 2 with some nonzero n), that would tell you exactly how many tracts have the problem, which is your starting point for troubleshooting.



Assuming everything looks OK, let’s move on. If not, we’d need to do some troubleshooting!

Area-Level (Tract-Level) Variables
These variables describe the census tract (geoid10) each participant lives in, rather than the participant individually — everyone living in the same tract shares the same value.

Population Density








Variable
Type

Traffic Volume
Variable: ctb1traff (Numeric — “Traffic density” per the official codebook)
Measured and estimated traffic volumes for major roads by road section are available annually from PennDOT (2005–present). Air pollution levels from traffic typically return to background levels within 100 to 300 m of roads. We calculated kernel densities of average daily traffic from PennDOT traffic data within 100 m and 300 m of road centerlines, on a 30 m grid, for southeastern Pennsylvania.

100 m was chosen based on work done for the New York City Community Air Survey.
300 m was chosen to account for the road width of wider roads.

The variable in the data set represents the average of the 100 m kernel-density average daily traffic in the participant’s residential census tract. Higher value = greater traffic volume.

title: Lesson 2: Reading a Published Conceptual Framework
text:
Introduction
This week’s Practice activity is a little different from a typical R tutorial. Instead of working through new code, you will work through a published paper — applying the vocabulary you just learned in the lectures (exposure, outcome, mediator, confounder, effect modifier) to decode a real framework from the environmental epidemiology literature.
The paper is:

Lachowycz K, Jones AP. (2013). Towards a better understanding of the relationship between greenspace and health: Development of a theoretical framework. Landscape and Urban Planning, 118, 62–69.







ImportantHow to use this tutorial



Work through the four parts in order — each builds on the one before it. Each part uses collapsible callout boxes to reveal answers after you have thought through each question yourself.
For the reflection questions: write your answers in your own words before you click to reveal the answer. The goal is to develop your reasoning, not produce the exact right phrasing.








NoteBefore you begin



Open the Lachowycz & Jones (2013) paper and find Figure 1 (the framework diagram on page 64 of the PDF). Keep it in front of you throughout Parts 1–4. Most of what you need is in that figure — the text provides context, but the diagram is the primary object you are working with.
One note on terminology: Lachowycz and Jones use the word moderator where this course uses effect modifier. These terms mean the same thing. A moderator changes the strength or direction of the main association across subgroups.





Part 1: Orient Yourself — Find the Core Hypothesis
Every framework, no matter how complex, starts with a simple two-box hypothesis: exposure → outcome. Before you try to read all the complexity in Figure 1, find that core.
1a. Looking at Figure 1, identify the core exposure and the core outcomes. Write them down in your own words.

What is the exposure? How is it measured?
What are the outcomes? How does the framework organize them?
Is the exposure measured at the individual level or the neighborhood/area level?

1b. In one sentence, state the hypothesis that Figure 1 is built around. Write it the way you would write a hypothesis for Milestone 1 — specific, directional, using “associated with.”






Note💡 Answer guide — click to reveal after attempting





1a.

Exposure: Access to greenspace — measured at the neighborhood or area level as distance to greenspace, amount of greenspace in the area, or similar spatial measures.
Outcomes: The framework distinguishes two broad categories: physical health (e.g., weight management, blood pressure, reduced risk of chronic disease) and psychological health (e.g., improved mental wellbeing, stress recovery, reduced aggression). These are shown as interacting rather than completely separate.
The exposure is area-level; outcomes are typically measured at the individual level.

1b. A reasonable hypothesis: Among urban residents, those living in neighborhoods with greater access to greenspace will have better physical and mental health outcomes, compared to those with lower greenspace access. Notice the need for “associated with” even here — Lachowycz and Jones are careful to describe their causal pathways as hypothetical.






Part 2: Identify the Mediators
The middle column of Figure 1 is labeled “Potential mediators.” These are variables on the causal pathway between the exposure and the outcomes — they explain how access to greenspace could improve health.
2a. The authors group the mediators into three broad categories. Identify and name those three categories from the figure.
2b. Pick one specific mediator from any of the three categories that makes intuitive sense to you. In 2–3 sentences, explain:

Where it sits in the causal story (exposure → mediator → outcome)
Why it belongs on the pathway rather than being a confounder

2c. The authors note in Section 2.2 that evidence for mediators “operating in practice remains elusive.” In your own words, why would that be the case? What would you need in order to actually test whether a mediator is operating?
(Hint: think about what a cross-sectional study can and cannot tell you about timing and sequence.)






Note💡 Answer guide — click to reveal after attempting





2a. The three mediator categories are:

Improved perceptions of the living environment (aesthetic satisfaction, sense of having the park there)
Aesthetic pleasure and relaxation from viewing greenspace
Use of greenspace — which includes relaxation activities, physical activities (jogging, football, playing), active travel (walking and cycling), interaction with wildlife, social interactions, and participation in group activities

2b. Any well-reasoned answer works. Example: Physical activity (a form of greenspace use) sits between greenspace access and physical health outcomes. It belongs on the pathway — not as a confounder — because it is caused by greenspace access and then causes improved health. A confounder would independently cause both greenspace access and health through a separate mechanism; a mediator is activated by the exposure itself.
2c. Cross-sectional studies measure the exposure, mediator, and outcome all at the same time. That means you cannot establish what came first — did living near greenspace lead to more physical activity, which then improved health? Or did healthier people choose to live near greenspace? To actually test mediation, you would ideally need longitudinal data where you measure changes in the mediator (e.g., physical activity levels) and the outcome over time in response to changes in the exposure — or a natural experiment where greenspace is introduced in an area and you can observe what happens next.






Part 3: Identify the Moderators (Effect Modifiers)
The left column of Figure 1 is labeled “Potential moderating factors.” These are variables that change the strength or direction of the greenspace–health association across different groups or contexts — what this course calls effect modifiers.
3a. The authors organize the moderating factors into three groups. Name the three groups as they appear in the figure.
3b. The authors argue that socioeconomic status (SES) can act as a moderator, not just a confounder. In plain language, what is the difference between those two claims? What would it mean for SES to modify the greenspace–health association, as opposed to confound it?
(Hint: think about what “adjusting for” a variable does in a regression model, versus what “stratifying by” a variable does.)
3c. Identify one moderating factor that you could examine using variables available in the class dataset. Name the variable you would use and describe what group comparison you would make.






Note💡 Answer guide — click to reveal after attempting





3a. The three groups of moderating factors are:

Demographic factors (age, gender, ethnicity, SES, occupation and lifestyle, household characteristics, dog ownership, car ownership)
Living context (cultural factors, community activity, safety and infrastructure, government policy, rural–urban setting, surface/greenery on routes)
Characteristics of green space (features, quality, maintenance/attractiveness, level and type of use, safety and privacy)

Climate is shown separately as a fourth column in the figure.
3b. Calling SES a confounder means: wealthier neighborhoods tend to have more greenspace AND lower disease rates through entirely separate mechanisms, so SES creates a spurious association that must be removed by adjusting for it in a model. Calling SES a moderator (effect modifier) means something different: the size of the greenspace–health benefit differs by SES level — for example, lower-SES residents may benefit more from greenspace access because they have fewer alternative health-promoting resources. The authors suggest both may be true simultaneously. Adjusting for SES (as a confounder) removes its confounding influence on the overall estimate; stratifying by SES (as a modifier) reveals whether the greenspace benefit is bigger or smaller in different groups.
3c. Several variables work. For example:

pov_allage (tract-level poverty proportion): you could compare the greenspace–health association in high-poverty versus low-poverty tracts
age: compare the association in younger versus older participants
female (0/1): compare the association by sex, as the paper discusses gender differences in greenspace use







Part 4: Read Critically — What Is Missing?
A conceptual framework is a theory about what matters. Part of reading a framework critically is noticing what it doesn’t include, and asking whether that matters.
4a. The authors acknowledge in their Discussion that the framework was built primarily from cross-sectional studies. Why does that matter? What types of causal claims does Figure 1 make that cross-sectional evidence cannot actually establish?
4b. The authors note one route of mediation that was deliberately excluded from the framework — the role of greenspace as a protector from environmental stressors such as pollution and heat (see the end of page 67 in the paper). Why did they exclude it? Do you agree with that decision, given what we now know about greenspace and air quality?






Note💡 Answer guide — click to reveal after attempting





4a. Cross-sectional studies measure everything at one point in time, making it impossible to establish what came first. Figure 1 uses arrows to imply temporal sequence and causal direction — but those arrows are theoretical claims, not conclusions from cross-sectional data. In particular, you cannot rule out reverse causation (healthier people choosing to live near greenspace) or confirm that the mediating variables operate in the sequence the diagram shows.
4b. The authors excluded it primarily because of insufficient epidemiological evidence at the time — not enough studies had directly tested it as a mechanism linking greenspace access to health outcomes in free-living populations. Whether that was the right call is worth debating: there is a plausible biological mechanism (trees absorb particulate matter, greenspace reduces urban heat island effects), and we now know considerably more about greenspace and air quality. Many researchers would argue this pathway deserves inclusion in updated versions of the framework — and indeed, the authors themselves suggest it “could potentially be incorporated” as evidence emerges.






Wrapping Up
The framework-reading skills you just applied — finding the exposure, outcome, mediators, and moderators in someone else’s published diagram — are exactly the skills you need to build your own framework for Milestone 1.
As you move into the Apply work, keep this in mind: every box in your framework needs a sentence of justification. Lachowycz and Jones wrote paragraphs for each element. Your Milestone 1 written explanation asks for one sentence per variable explaining why it is there and what role it plays — the same kind of reasoning, at a smaller scale.

title: Lesson 4: Exposure Assessment & Misclassification
text:
In Lesson 3 you cleaned and characterized your variables — checking distributions, catching implausible values, and visualizing what you had. This lesson asks a question that comes before all of that: how good is the exposure measurement itself?
Every environmental exposure in this course — NDVI, tree canopy, traffic density, poverty — is a proxy. None of it is a direct measurement of what actually reached a person’s lungs, skin, or bloodstream. That gap between the true exposure and what we actually measured is called exposure misclassification, and it is not a minor technical footnote — it changes what your effect estimates mean and, in some cases, which direction they’re biased in.
Even before that gap enters the picture, you face a second decision that’s easy to overlook: once you have a continuous exposure measurement — say, an NDVI value for every participant — how should you actually use it in your analysis? Leave it as a continuous number? Split it into a few categories, like “low/medium/high”? Collapse it into just two groups, “high” vs. “low”? This is called an exposure coding decision, and it is not just a formatting choice: it trades off how much statistical power you have to detect a real association, whether you can detect a relationship that isn’t a simple straight line, and how easy your results are to interpret and communicate. Different coding choices can even lead to different conclusions from the same underlying data — which is exactly why the decision needs to be made thoughtfully and justified, not just defaulted to.
This lesson has two parts:

title: Lesson 4: Exposure Assessment & Misclassification
text:
Why coding decisions matter
Suppose you measure a continuous exposure — NDVI, ozone, traffic density, whatever it is. You now face a choice that has nothing to do with the biology of the exposure and everything to do with how you plan to model it:

Leave it continuous?
Split it into a small number of categories (tertiles, quartiles)?
Dichotomize it into two groups (high/low)?









Approach
What you gain
What you lose




Continuous (keep the raw numbers)
You keep every bit of information in the data, which gives you the best chance of detecting a real association if one exists — this is what people mean by “more statistical power.” You can also model curved (not just straight-line) relationships if you use the right tools.
By default, a regression model assumes the relationship is a straight line (more exposure = proportionally more risk, all the way up and down the scale) unless you specifically tell it otherwise. A single number (“for each 1-unit increase in exposure…”) can also be harder to explain to a general audience than “low/medium/high.”


Categorical (3+ groups, e.g., quartiles or tertiles)
You can see whether risk jumps around unevenly across the range of exposure — for example, if only the highest group has meaningfully higher risk — without assuming a straight-line relationship. Easier to describe in plain language (“low/medium/high exposure”).
You need enough people in each group for your results to be reliable, and where exactly you draw the group boundaries is somewhat arbitrary.


Binary (high vs. low)
The simplest possible result to interpret and explain: two groups, one comparison.
You throw away the most information — everyone in “low” is treated as identical, even someone barely below the cutoff and someone far below it. Depending on where you draw the line, you can make a real relationship look stronger, weaker, or disappear entirely.



There is no single correct answer. The right choice depends on your research question, how many participants you have, what prior studies suggest about the shape of the relationship, and — sometimes — a threshold that already has real-world meaning (e.g., the EPA’s ground-level ozone standard of 70 ppb over an 8-hour average). Whatever you choose, the decision should be transparent and justified, not just whatever produced the most convenient result.

Participant-level vs. city-level distribution of NDVI
Because our study participants don’t live in a random sample of Philadelphia’s 384 census tracts — they live where they live — the distribution of NDVI among participants can differ from the distribution across the city. If certain tracts are over- or under-represented in who happened to enroll, our sample may not reflect the full range of greenness found citywide.

Note💡 Discussion — click to reveal after you’ve looked at both summaries yourself





The two distributions turn out to be quite similar. Citywide, NDVI ranges from about -0.03 to 0.35 (median ≈ 0.13); among participants, it ranges from about -0.03 to 0.35 as well (median ≈ 0.12) — nearly identical minimums and maximums, with the participant distribution’s median and mean each only slightly lower than the city’s. Participants also turn out to live in 363 of the city’s 384 tracts (about 95% of them) — not a narrow slice of the city at all.
That’s good news for this particular exposure: it means our study sample is exposed to nearly the full range of greenness found across Philadelphia, so conclusions about NDVI from this dataset are likely to generalize reasonably well to the city as a whole. Had the two distributions looked very different instead — say, if participants were clustered in only the greenest (or only the least green) tracts — we’d be looking at a narrower slice of the exposure range than actually exists in the population, which would limit how confidently we could generalize our findings city-wide, and could also make it harder to detect a dose-response relationship if most of our variation in exposure were compressed into a small range.

What do you gain by dichotomizing (simplicity of interpretation)? What do you lose (variability, statistical power, the ability to detect a dose-response pattern)?
Would a fixed threshold — say, NDVI > 0.3, chosen based on prior literature rather than this sample’s own median — ever make more sense than a data-driven split? When would you want a threshold that doesn’t depend on your own sample?







Note💡 Discussion — click to reveal after you’ve tried both splits yourself





Median vs. mean split: the median split comes out almost perfectly even (1,008 vs. 992 — essentially half and half, which is exactly what a median split guarantees by definition). The mean split is noticeably less even (1,104 vs. 896). That gap tells you something about the shape of the distribution: the mean (≈ 0.131) is a bit higher than the median (≈ 0.120), which happens when a distribution is right-skewed — most tracts cluster at low-to-moderate NDVI, with a smaller number of much-greener tracts pulling the mean upward. Because more of the sample sits below that higher mean value, fewer participants end up in the “high” group under a mean split.
What you gain and lose by dichotomizing: you gain simplicity — a single “high vs. low” comparison is about as easy to interpret and communicate as a result gets. You lose the variation within each group (someone just barely above the cutoff is treated identically to someone with the highest NDVI in the whole sample), which costs you statistical power and can hide a dose-response pattern entirely — if risk actually climbs gradually across the full range of NDVI, a single high/low split will only ever show you the average difference between the two halves, not the shape of that climb.
Fixed threshold vs. data-driven split: a sample-based split (median or mean) is relative to this dataset — the “high” group here might not be “high” in a different city or a different sample. A fixed threshold grounded in prior literature or a policy standard (like NDVI > 0.3, or the EPA’s ozone standard) instead reflects a threshold that means something on its own, independent of your sample, which makes your results more directly comparable across studies and often more directly relevant to policy. You’d reach for a fixed threshold when that kind of external comparability matters more than describing this particular sample’s own internal distribution.

section: A simulated dataset where we know the truth
text:
A simulated dataset where we know the truth
In a real study we never observe the true exposure alongside the misclassified one — if we could measure the true value, we wouldn’t have a misclassification problem. So how can we possibly show what misclassification does to an estimate?
By using simulated data. A simulated dataset isn’t collected from real people at all — it’s generated by a computer program that follows rules a researcher specifies in advance. For example: “asthma risk increases with true ozone exposure according to this exact mathematical formula, and then a second, ‘measured’ version of ozone is created by adding some random noise to the true value.” The “participants” aren’t real children, but the relationships in the data are built to resemble a real study closely enough to be a useful stand-in for one. The advantage is total control: because we wrote the rules, we already know the ground truth — the true relationship between ozone and asthma, and exactly how the misclassified versions were generated from it — something that is never available in a real dataset. That lets us compare “true” results against “misclassified” results directly, which is exactly what we need to see misclassification’s consequences with our own eyes rather than just taking the theory on faith.
To see those consequences, we’ll use a dataset built specifically for this purpose: 500 simulated children in Philadelphia, with doctor-diagnosed asthma (yes/no) as the outcome and three versions of the same ozone exposure — the true value, and two different misclassified versions.

A reminder: how is tree canopy coded?
Before modeling an exposure, remind yourself what its values mean and what its distribution looks like — you characterized this in Lesson 3, and it matters again here.

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
A few things to keep in mind about hrlctree:

It is a proportion, from 0 to 1: a value of 0.12 means 12% of the participant’s census tract is covered by tree canopy. In our data it ranges from about 0.02 (2%) to 0.63 (63%), with a median of about 0.12 (12%).
It is measured at the census-tract level, not for each person: every participant who lives in the same tract has the same value. The 2,000 participants live in 363 tracts.
It is right-skewed: most participants live in tracts with 5–20% canopy, and a small number live in much greener tracts. Keep this in mind in Part 2 — it affects how wide each quartile is.

Step 1: Categorize tree canopy into quartiles

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
ntile(hrlctree, 4) sorts participants from lowest to highest tree canopy and splits them into four groups of (nearly) equal size — 500 participants each:

Q1 — the 25% of participants living in the least green tracts (about 2% to 8% canopy)
Q2 — the next 25% (about 8% to 12% canopy)
Q3 — the next 25% (about 12% to 18% canopy)
Q4 — the 25% of participants living in the greenest tracts (about 18% to 63% canopy)

Notice that the quartiles have equal numbers of people, not equal ranges of canopy: because canopy is right-skewed, Q4 spans a much wider range of canopy (about 45 percentage points) than Q1–Q3 combined (about 16).
Look at the last column: prevalence of high blood pressure is about 35–36% in Q1 and Q2, 31% in Q3, and 20% in Q4.

Step 2: Fit the model with quartiles as indicator terms

Please enable JavaScript to experience the dynamic code cell content on this page.
Wrapping the quartile variable in factor() is what tells R to create a separate indicator term for each category. Without it, R treats 1, 2, 3, 4 as a continuous number and returns a single coefficient — which would assume linearity instead of testing it.
What “ref = Q1” means. With a categorical exposure, R needs a reference category that every other category is compared with. By default it uses the first level — here, Q1, the least green quartile. Q1 therefore does not get its own row in the output: its PR is 1 by definition. Each PR you see is the prevalence of high blood pressure in that quartile divided by the prevalence in Q1. That is why every interpretation below says “compared with participants in the lowest quartile.”
Interpreting the results:








Quartile

Interpretation

The comparison group for every other row


Q2 (8–12%)
1.03 (0.87, 1.22)
Prevalence essentially the same as Q1 (3% higher). The CI includes 1, so the data are consistent with no difference.


Q3 (12–18%)
0.89 (0.74, 1.06)
Prevalence 11% lower than Q1, but the CI still includes 1, so this could plausibly be no difference.


Q4 (18–63%)
0.58 (0.47, 0.72)
Prevalence 42% lower than Q1. The whole CI is below 1: the data are not consistent with no difference.



In words, for Q4: the prevalence of high blood pressure among participants living in the greenest quarter of tracts was 0.58 times the prevalence among those in the least green quarter (95% CI: 0.47, 0.72).
